To avoid this, we establish a large-step operational semantics that interprets computations as single, composite operations. This is achieved by applying the monotonic Kripke model construction to a small-step semantics modified with a totalisation axiom. This states that a program will indefinitely loop if it is able to execute n times without reaching a halt. This framework has been proven to be equivalent to the small-step semantics for a specific language model, thereby providing a theoretical foundation for large-step operational semantics. , the Discrete Granular Cell Carney problem, has been proven to be unresolvable in the one-way model with a poly(n) size input. We have established a relationship between its resolved instances and Merkle's problem, thereby restricting the possible solutions to instances with at most Ω(n log n) size. Given that Merkle's problem can be solved in the one-way model with exactly n bits, Discrete Granular Cell Carney's complete set of instances can be solved under the same conditions, with a modified approach that involves splitting the input into two equal parts. We have also shown that if Discrete Granular Cell Carney's complete set of instances can be solved in the one-way model with a way more complex (super-polynomial) size, then the resolution would contradict a fundamental theorem. The same reasoning can be applied to a series of problems derived from Discrete Granular Cell Carney's instances. On the other hand, Discrete Granular Cell Carney's partial solution can help solve a Merkle-related problem in the one-way model with a probabilistic component, thereby contributing to our understanding of limits to knowledge in a distributed setting. The same trade-off has been observed when trying to solve Merkle's problem partially, with the added effect that a lower bound for a distributed version of Merkle's problem can be derived from a lower bound for Discrete Granular Cell Carney's partial solution. We have also established a connection between the lower bounds in communication complexity and multi-party problems that involve arithmetic operations, showing that a multi-party lower bound can imply a similar lower bound in the context of communication complexity, particularly for problems with a two-party setup. Based on this relationship, any progress towards solving known multi-party lower bounds that involve arithmetic operations would also yield progress towards solving a variant of Discrete Granular Cell Carney's, thereby yielding bounds that are comparable to a complex number system, with a modified set of operations. We have also derived lower bounds for multi-party problems that involve arithmetic operations in a controlled number of parties setting, with a complex number system, and we have shown that a variant of Discrete Granular Cell Carney's, with a modified set of operations, can be solved in a four-party one-way model with a size of O(n^(1/3)). We have used the obtained lower bounds to solve a variant of Discrete Granular Cell Carney's, with a modified set of operations, partially in a three-party one-way model with a complexity of Ω(n). We identify the groups that can be formed as groups of deck transformations of iterations of such bicritical maps, providing a comprehensive classification up to isomorphism. This classification is also extended to dynamical systems defined by rational functions of any degree, also known as rational dynamical systems, under certain constraints on the denominator. A typical explanation for this effect points to the trapping and release of charge defects, but this perspective doesn't fully account for the observed behavior. In this study, we propose a new mathematical framework, beyond Bloch's theorem, to help with analyses of insulating materials that don't fit into the traditional approach. By using a new mathematical tool, we can break down the band structure into three main parts: the first is a natural, built-in part that still adheres to traditional theories; the second is a part that reflects how the band structure changes due to irregularities on tiny scales; and the third represents massive gravitational effects that can't be broken down further. In conclusion, our new approach provides a more comprehensive understanding of materials that can't fit into traditional theories and helps uncover new topological properties of these materials. Researchers have been investigating constraint screening, a technique that can expedite the solution process for large-scale unit commitment problems by reducing the number of unnecessary constraints. Current constraint screening methods rely on optimizing load and generation, but this approach tends to be conservative and leaves a considerable percentage of constraints intact. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a machine learning-based model to predict costs given load inputs, enabling more effective optimization and constraint screening in unit commitment problems. By incorporating cost perspectives and machine learning, the proposed model outperforms conventional approaches, significantly reducing computational time across various scenarios. Furthermore, this paper demonstrates the value of incorporating economic perspectives in constraint screening for large-scale optimization problems. While primarily focused on unit commitment, the proposed model can also be applied to other optimization problems involving costs, such as optimal power flow and generation expansion planning. Importantly, this paper introduces novel datasets tailored to unit commitment and optimal power flow, serving as valuable resources for further constraint screening research. Moreover, we developed a spiking neural network counterpart to the proposed algorithm, which learns a safety-critical path in an unknown environment. Experimental results from both simulation and real-world robotic experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in developing reliable robotic motion planning strategies. This work presents a novel framework for learning a safety-critical neural motion planning model using a deep reinforcement learning approach, which combines supervised and reinforcement learning techniques. This approach incorporates constraints from physics simulators to define the state space and ensure that the learned policies respect system constraints. By leveraging this approach, neural motion planning models are developed that demonstrate equivalent performance to traditional algorithms while increasing functionality. For instance, in the airbrushing task, the learned policies from the novel framework led to 85% of paths being barrier-free, a 0.6% increase over previous methods. Moreover, when integrated into the AirLab lab's device pipeline, the novel framework enables real-time conversion of human intentions into safe robotic motions, reducing processing time to 100 milliseconds. Numerical verification of these results was conducted to verify the system's safety and feasibility. Moreover, we demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach in developing explainable AI models by conducting AI model auditing, which increased the model's transparency by 0.6 and 0.3 standard deviations, respectively. Moreover, neural networks trained using this approach achieve 100% barrier-free path rate in the Airbrushing task, 100 ms processing time in the device pipeline, and 0.9 standard deviation reduction in the target position accuracy. These results show that the novel framework can develop reliable, explainable, and effective spiking neural network-based motion planners. Specifically, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula have emerged as valuable tools in this effort. Furthermore, the superbosonization formula was utilized to derive an exact free-energy expression for 2x2 matrix $\beta J^2$ commutation relations, providing an alternative to previously established results obtained by other methods. In addition to its independent interest, the excellent agreement between this new expression and Monte Carlo simulations highlights the potential of the superbosonization formula as a precise and computationally efficient surrogate for Monte Carlo simulations in certain scenarios. In a broader context, the integration of supersymmetric methods into matrix integrals of the type involved in disordered systems and string theory's AdS/CFT correspondence may be achieved via the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, allowing the construction of nested Wilson-Fisher fixed points. Notably, the theoretical framework has also given rise to a new evaluation method for the inverse bosonic Moyal bracket. In an unrelated context, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation has been applied to derive a supersymmetric representation of the iterated Toda integrals that define the string background for certain operators in $\mathcal{N}=1$ supergravity. In this specific context, the transformation has facilitated the derivation of a compendium of previously known macroscopic string backgrounds constructed through the iteration of theta functions' determinants. In addition to its independent interest, this supersymmetric representation may enable the development of novel methods for general index computations for one-loop Wilson loops in Seiberg-Wilson theories via a connection to the elliptic Selberg integral established in this work. In a separate context, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation has also been applied to a specific type of superconformal field theory recently connected to the gravitational dual via a Rehmann-Sherman-Thompson like duality. In this particular scenario, the supersymmetric representation of the supercharge's one-loop beta function receives corrections from explicit supersymmetry breaking terms. In an attempt to restore the original supersymmetry, a new mechanism has been proposed, based on the superbosonization formula, which uses a bosonic auxiliary matrix to restore the supersymmetry by equating it to a fermionic matrix with a specific jump distribution. In contrast to the existing dualities, the theoretical framework achieves the supersymmetry restoration at the one-loop level without requiring the equivalence of the gravitational and field-theoretic degrees of freedom.

Current research has sought to automatically enhance taxonomies by learning concept representations in Euclidean space. However, the natural geometric structure of taxonomies aligns better with hyperbolic properties, making this space more suitable for representation. We propose HyperExpan, an algorithm that preserves hierarchical structure and semantic relationships by projecting a taxonomy into a hyperbolic embedding space. This approach utilizes graph neural networks to capture semantic relations and temporal convolution networks to capture hierarchical dependencies. The results of our experiments demonstrate that HyperExpan outperforms traditional methods, achieving better accuracy with a smaller required training dataset. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art or competitive results on four benchmark taxonomies, including YAGO, NELL, UML, and WordNet. The HyperExpan code is publicly available at https://github.com/HongmingChang/HongmingChang.git.

C,(σ,1) = σ(Lecho(1), Lecho(1)),(2)

The temporal convolution network used to capture hierarchical dependencies in HyperExpan is defined as follows: 

H,(T,1) = T(Lecho(|T|), Lecho(|T|)),(3)

where H represents the target hyperbolic convolution result, (T,1) represents the target hyperbolic convolution, and the function |T| represents the number of concepts in the target hyperbolic convolution.

We introduce a novel framework for evaluating system resiliency based on a specific logical structure called a Resiliency Specification, which is comprised of STL formulas. By integrating time bounds and combining individual components, this framework provides an in-depth analysis of a system's ability to rapidly recover and maintain stability. By analyzing large radio source samples from 1.4 GHz surveys, this study calculates the median fractional polarization in relation to angular size. It finds a strong correlation between polarization and source size below 5", with a weaker correlation above 8". The results indicate depolarization due to the host galaxy and surrounding environment. Additionally, the curvature of low-frequency radio spectra shows an inverse correlation with polarization. It is speculated that this might be due to total flux density weighted source size or the presence of strong depolarizing gradients. Using cosmological density fluctuations as a framework, a depolarization scale of approximately 5" is predicted for sources above 0.1 Jy at 1.4 GHz, with more intense and curved spectra experiencing greater depolarization. This analysis predicts nearly 100% depolarization for sources over 20", with a 50% depolarization scale, indicating a more severe depolarization problem for future experiments like PERSQUEE and POLOS. It is considered challenging for individual source modeling, requiring a more comprehensive approach like cross-correlation analysis to mitigate systematic effects from AGN radio source depolarization. This representation accurately captures turbulence's essence, characterized by the shift from one coherent structure to another. Our analysis yields exact expressions for the turbulent transport operator without employing simplifying assumptions. In the limit where spatial and temporal locality prevail, our operator reduces to the conventional estimate of turbulent transport. Furthermore, we test the stability of this reduction in simplified scenarios, and our findings suggest that small modifications to the velocity field can significantly impact transport even at large scales. In particular, the effects of spatial and temporal locality are most vulnerable to perturbations in the vicinity of equilibrium states and regions with extreme velocity gradients. Additionally, we explore the stochastic properties of turbulent transport and establish that coherent structures can act as diffusive traps, trapping particles and enhancing transport at specific scales. Finally, we demonstrate that turbulent transport remains finite when the velocity field's spatial and temporal components are correlated, under the condition that the structure function decays at large scales at a rate faster than $l^{-a}$ for some positive $a$. This condition, however, is insufficient to guarantee finite transport when the velocity field's time series is red with a finite correlation time. In such instances, turbulent transport may diverge or converge, depending on the specific dynamics of the flow. the task of jointly selecting users and precoding can be reformulated as recovering a group-sparse signal from underdetermined equations. Building on this reformulation, the paper introduces an algorithm grounded in the group LASSO approach. Relative to the existing solutions, the proposed method achieves two key improvements: higher attainable sum-rate values and lower interference at inactive user devices. Specifically, the algorithm resolves the design challenge in two distinct phases, first constructing a set of possible user selections and then generating a closed-form optimization solution within this candidate pool. The algorithm's efficacy is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical simulations that highlight its benefits relative to the state-of-the-art solutions. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm is successfully integrated into a multi-cell MIMO system, ensuring efficient and stable operation. Notably, the algorithm's compatibility with generic solvers enables its adaptation to various optimization objectives beyond the sum-rate metric. The computational experiments validate the algorithm's ability to achieve a higher sum-rate value of 13.22 nbits/second/Hz, representing a 1.16-fold increase over the baseline solution based on ZF precoding. The proposed algorithm is also resilient to interference from adjacent cells, with computational experiments demonstrating interference reduction by a factor of 10 or more, particularly when the algorithm is applied in multi-cell environments with opposing user selections. The average power consumption of the proposed algorithm is significantly lower, at most 1.16 times that of the baseline solution. The computational overhead of the proposed algorithm is expected to increase by a factor of 1.24 to 1.33, with the actual computational overhead depending on the specific optimization objective and configuration parameters. The proposed algorithm is compatible with a range of optimization objectives, with the most beneficial objective being the sum-rate metric. The potential integration of the proposed algorithm into established mobile network standards is discussed. Originally built using Gabidulin codes over $F_q(t)$, Loidreau's system was found to be vulnerable to three distinct attacks.
This study proposes a code-switching modification and a matrix-form modification to address these vulnerabilities.
The first modification combines two encodings with different properties to create a secure system.
The second modification transforms the Gabidulin matrix used for multiplication into a secure, symmetric matrix.
Both modifications maintain the original plaintext space and decryption function, but modify the ciphertext matrix and decryption oracle, respectively.
As a result, the proposed modifications offer a secure alternative to Loidreau's original system.
Furthermore, the study examines a secure instantiation of another code-based cryptosystem built using the optimal normal basis (ONB) technique. 
This secure instantiation is presented as an alternative to Loidreau's system. 
Both modifications and the secure instantiation were demonstrated using concrete examples in the form of (binary, ternary) code-based cryptosystems. 
This study also explores two potential applications for code-based cryptosystems: one involves the measurement device, and the other exploits quantum computers. 
As quantum sources become more prevalent, the measurement attack may become the primary code-based attack in the future. 
Consequently, this study aims to enhance the security of code-based cryptosystems against measurement attacks by employing super-dense coding.
By applying the conventional dense coding method, the study constructs a secure multiple-function key-exchange protocol to counter measurement attacks. 
As an alternative to the dense coding method, the study presents a secure code-based key-exchange protocol using ONB, thereby limiting attacker capacity and increasing secure data transmission. 
Both the dense coding method and the ONB approach were demonstrated through concrete examples of binary and ternary code-based cryptosystems. 
This study also examines the possibility of enhancing the security of code-based cryptosystems against quantum attacks by applying quantum computations. 
As quantum computers can efficiently solve the Hilbert curve problem (HCP), which involves searching for similar components in code-based cryptosystems, they can potentially break these systems.
To counter this threat, the study introduces two modifications for strengthening the security of code-based cryptosystems against quantum attacks. 
This study employs the quantum computations of the lower bound of the largest prime divisor (QLB) function, which involves factoring polynomials over $F_q(t)$, to increase the level of difficulty for attackers and protect the code-based systems.

The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training cycle. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling techniques have several shortcomings. Primarily, they expand the label set cautiously by choosing only the most confident, yet potentially uninformative nodes, which merely amplify minor improvements. Secondly, they combine pseudo-labels with actual labels using the same loss function, failing to acknowledge their distinct contributions. When executed in parallel, SGD demands communication among involved processes at each iteration. Our innovation is a communication-efficient approach that minimizes communication during SGD by utilizing a specific data division strategy and optimizing the computation of gradients in parallel. The former involves assigning data subsets to process groups based on the volume of gradients, which can be updated without requiring communication. The latter is achieved by distributing samples based on a factorial design, which naturally yields conditional independence among sample subsets and allows parallel computation of expectations, ultimately enabling the computation of gradients without the need for communication after a initial iteration. We establish that any hypergraph can be viewed as a composition of hypergraphs formed by a common tensor-based operation. This operation allows us to identify and create novel hypergraph structures, such as hypercycles and hyparabolic graphs. Additionally, we define a generalization of the cycle graph and demonstrate that a given hypergraph is hyparic if and only if it does not contain a specific substructure. Furthermore, we obtain descriptions of the spectral properties of the tensor-based operation and show that the adjacency matrix of hypergraphs formed by this operation inherits the regularity and spectral properties of the constituent hypergraphs. Several illustrative examples are provided to demonstrate the concepts introduced in this paper. Finally, some open problems and potential applications are outlined. These include connections to the study of generalized determinant, rank-related problems for higher-order tensors, and the possibility of extending established concepts from graph theory to the realm of hypergraphs. We suggest exploring hypergraph projections as a promising approach for investigating various hypergraph configurations. Specifically, we define a projection of a $d$-uniform $m$-vertex hypergraph as a new hypergraph obtained by removing or combining vertices while maintaining the existing $k$-size subsets, but also allowing for the creation of new ones, if possible. We establish some general criteria and provide a few initial results regarding necessary and sufficient conditions for such projections to exist. Finally, we identify a fundamental limitation in this context: even very small hypergraphs do not admit projections, while we show that any $d$-uniform hypergraph with at least $(d+1)(m-1)$ vertices can indeed be projected, thus establishing a partial characterization of the sufficiency condition for a projection to exist. Nevertheless, confusion networks (a more complex set of possible outcomes than a shortlist) can be a compact representation of the potential outcomes of the system.  We investigate in this study the advantages of using confusion networks instead of a shortlist of the top ASR hypotheses when processing ASR outcomes.  We show that using confusion networks can be beneficial in two ways: by enabling a more detailed understanding of dialogue history by considering adjacent outcomes and by streamlining the development of dialogue systems by integrating the processing of ASR outcomes and dialogue management for a single pass processing of speech without needing to first translate the output into text.  We test this approach using the Switchboard and Safari datasets and compare the results with the standard method of processing ASR hypotheses in order to evaluate the impact on system performance in domain-independent dialogue systems.  We find that the system processing confusion networks achieves a 0.8 point increase in average turn accuracy, 0.3 point decrease in average turn latency, and improved domain-independent dialogue system performance when tested using the SLD task when processing confusion networks as opposed to a shortlist of the top ASR hypotheses.  Furthermore, integrating the processing of ASR outcomes and dialogue management in a single pass processing of speech results in a significant reduction in parameter count from over 126 to approximately 31 when processing confusion networks as opposed to a shortlist of the top ASR hypotheses.  We also found that translating confusion networks into text results in a loss of information which could result in a system performance deterioration of as much as 0.6 when processing the text as opposed to the original confusion network text.  We conclude that integrating the processing of ASR outcomes and dialogue management in a single pass processing of speech, and using confusion networks instead of a shortlist of the top ASR hypotheses, can benefit the development of domain-independent dialogue systems.  We offer the confusion network processing method in a publicly accessible software package, and the associated project data can be viewed at the specified link. researchers have focused on tackling the pervasive issue of hate speech online. This pernicious problem gives rise to real-world consequences, such as escalated violence, which is exacerbated by the global reach of social networks. The limited availability of dataset annotations in hate speech detection, particularly in English, hampers the generalization of models to other languages, such as Arabic and German. Previous studies on hate speech classification have primarily relied on tree-based models and traditional machine learning methods. Nonetheless, recent studies on hate speech have introduced novel techniques, such as transfer learning and graph neural networks. Nonetheless, a comprehensive comparison of these approaches remains a gap in the literature. The primary aim of this research is to evaluate the performance of various architectures in hate speech classification tasks. We have integrated advanced language modeling techniques, such as transfer learning and graph neural networks, to enhance existing models' performance. Our experimental findings reveal that adding node and edge features to Graph Convolutional Networks significantly improves the performance of existing models. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the efficacy of using ensemble methods on German and Arabic datasets. Notably, we have broken new ground with state-of-the-art results on the Antidemagógia, DW16, and XMURDER datasets, as well as achieving impressive improvements on the Out of Vocabulary and Out of Distribution benchmarks. The code used in this research will be made publicly available to facilitate future studies. The new architecture, dubbed XMURDER-GCN, has been designed to integrate graph convolutional layers, attention mechanisms, and pooling layers to empower hate speech classification. The code supplements existing architectures by incorporating techniques such as dataset augmentation to combat Out of Vocabulary challenges, as well as leveraging Graph Convolutional Layers to capture relational information from the training dataset. The enhanced code, which integrates monitoring and visualization tools to automate the process of identifying the optimal number of node and edge features, has been optimized to increase the transparency of the model's predictions, as well as its performance. When optimizing smooth, strongly-convex functions with condition number $\kappa$, we 
prove that $T$ iterations of SGD with step sizes that decrease exponentially and 
knowing the function's smoothness achieve $\tilde{O}\left(\exp \left(

In order to improve their performance in out-of-distribution environments, it is crucial to develop training strategies that incentivize the extraction of relevant features early on in the training process.  In this study, we explore how the use of simple task-switching during training affects the ability of deep neural networks to switch between tasks and how it impacts performance in out-of-distribution environments. Ultimately, we conclude that incorporating task-switching in training, either explicitly or implicitly through the encouragement of feature extraction, is a promising strategy for extracting relevant features from data quickly, which in turn improves the ability of deep neural networks to adapt to new situations.  In the process, we also develop a novel dataset to test generalization and perform several case studies to gain a deeper understanding of feature extraction in various tasks.  Moreover, we propose a novel method to improve the ability of deep neural networks to adapt to new environments by incorporating human insights to identify relevant features from data quickly as well. A new algorithm, BID2, builds upon the Ssing approach, incorporating the kernel's singular structure and applying minimax optimization between predictions and singularly constrained blur kernels. A extension of the Ssing method, BID2 tackles each kernel's singular structure separately, achieving speedup by leveraging the sparse structure of singular kernels and using tabu methods to further boost performance, a research first in the context of blind image deblurring. A combination of interior point methods and tabu search ensures the convergence to a singular kernel approximating the kernel's shape, an optimization strategy never before applied to blind image deblurring. compositional semantic parsing of declarative language assertions.

verification against domain-specific safety requirements specified in everyday

One advantage of this approach is its versatility in handling problems with multiple radiation channels, regardless of bandwidth, mode dispersion, or interaction structure. Our method also allows us to study complex multi-photon scattering problems that cannot be solved using traditional methods. Furthermore, we extend this technique to more complex systems involving multiple emitters by providing an exact set of equations for two and three-photon scattering operators. This theoretical framework is applied to a specific example: the experimental study of four-photon scattering in driven quantum harmonic systems. By comparing our predictions with numerical simulations, we identify the conditions necessary for these systems to exhibit non-standard photon behavior in the presence of delays. Crucially, we find that with reasonable microwave engineering, two-photon scattering matrices can be approximated by single-photon matrices, but three-photon matrices inevitably display deviations from single-photon behavior. However, with the aid of delays, we demonstrate that these systems can either purely transmit or absorb photons, effectively exhibiting non-standard behavior. Our work offers a powerful tool for the analysis of more complex multi-photon processes in quantum systems that utilize delayed quantum feedback. Moreover, it outlines a clear pathway for the realization of non-standard photon behavior in four or more photon states, a crucial requirement for the processing of complex multi-photon signals. Popular techniques for anomaly detection rely on various distance metrics to identify differences between data entries. Each distance metric produces distinct results based on its mathematical characteristics, but there isn't a unified method to combine them. In this context, for noisy maximally entangled states $\psi$, one-round quantum games can be interpreted as having a constant quantum lower bound $L_{Q}(\Gamma)$, essentially exceeding their classical counterpart $L_{C}(\Gamma)$. (A/B Testing) a gold standard for several decades. Many companies use a standard framework that measures "average treatment effect" (ATE), but there's a significant challenge: excluding influential "outlier" participants who distort the results. There's a lack of reliable and easily implementable methods to identify these participants. While various methods have been developed to assign "weights" reducing their influence, these methods are often complicated, unreliable, or unaffordable for small samples. This study provides a clear and straightforward method to identify and exclude influential participants. Although the weights methods can be challenging to implement, we show that using simple differences in means can effectively identify these participants. This approach is easy to apply, provides reliable accuracy, and works well with small samples. By incorporating this method into the standard framework, the results will be more accurate and trustworthy. By applying this method, the variance of the estimated effect is reduced and the influence of each participant is evenly considered. We validated our approach by using data from 22 company experiments involving 100,000 or more participants. In most cases, excluding a relatively small number of participants (around 0.1%) significantly improves the accuracy of the estimated effect. In some cases, excluding 1% or more of participants yields a significantly improved accuracy. This approach is easily accessible to researchers who run controlled experiments in industry settings. By using this method, experimenters can provide a reliable and evenly applicable estimate of the treatment effect, and we suggest reporting the estimated effect after excluding participants as "outliers". Deep Space transport is presented, utilizing a cutting-edge Gas Core Reactor (GCR) integrated with a magnetohydrodynamic generator. A novel GCR design with enhanced characteristics compared to existing models is proposed and validated, capable of generating 200 MW of electricity within a 200 ton system. This GCR consists of a spherical cavity within a molybdenum-92 enclosure surrounded by a 50 cm thick liquid beryllium reflector, utilizing a fuel mix consisting of 235 UF4, KF, and K. Numerical simulations reveal that the system functions optimally within pressure ranges of 50 to 100 atm. Detailed neutronic assessments were conducted via Monte-Carlo modeling, resulting in crucial insights for determining the required reactor pressure, size, and moderator thickness. Additionally, the study calculates the thermal conductivity of superheated fuel under varying temperature and pressure conditions. The findings suggest that space propulsion requires maintaining the reactor at critical thresholds, ensuring kinetic balance between the positive and negative modes. Consequently, the minimum reactor pressure is estimated at 51.2 atm, while maximizing pressure would only increment the thermal efficiency by 4%. Moreover, the study determines that minimizing pressure and hence weight, can be achieved by increasing the reflectivity of the moderator by optimizing the reflector's thickness. However, when the moderator thickness exceeds 120 cm, reflectivity plateaus and diminishes. The analysis of space propulsion requires distinguishing between the thermodynamic limit and entropy-driven degradation in battery performance. Numerical simulations indicate that the maximum electrical output from the GCR is 204 MW, while actual power generation would be slightly lower due to radiation-induced degradation in the battery. The numerical models for electrical and thermodynamic properties of space propulsion components were validated using GenieMC and REMC Monte-Carlo modeling, with the results suggesting a need for maintaining fuel-moderator contact to prevent superheating and hence ensure optimal performance. The study estimates that the minimum thickness of the moderator needed to facilitate this contact is 16 cm, with the height of fluid layers exceeding the reactor cavity by 6.3 m in gravity. Nonetheless, in the absence of gravitational forces, the height of fluid layers would not pose an issue, allowing the reactor to function optimally when pressures are within the 50 to 100 atm range. The detailed analysis of GCR systems designed for Deep Space transport has yielded several crucial insights for optimizing nuclear power systems: first, the minimum pressure and hence weight of such systems can be optimized by increasing the reflectivity of the moderator;

We explore two specific scenarios: one focusing on the relationship between bulk and corner states, and the other examining edge and corner correlations. We establish the existence of mobility gaps for bulk-corner correspondence and clarify the topological properties defining these gaps. Interestingly, our study reveals that while bulk-corner correspondence remains intact even with disorder, corner states are safeguarded by mobility gaps rather than the overall bulk gaps. On the other hand, for edge-corner correspondence, our analysis demonstrates that both bulk and edge mobility gaps no longer guarantee the protection of edge and corner states in the presence of disorder. We find a new type of phase transition in this scenario, which we refer to as the "exceptional phase transition," and show that this transition can occur without closing the bulk or edge mobility gaps. A key feature of this transition is the permanent occupation of a specific edge or corner state, which is linked to the correspondence between edges and corners. depends on intricate electronic transport mechanisms involving the constituent

conductivity: by scattering electrons, they can hinder it but can also enhance it
by facilitating electron propagation through a complex energy terrain. 
In our investigation, we have observed a temperature-dependent, coherent electron
transfer between neighboring nanotubes through measurements of conductivity on
an armchair single-wall carbon nanotube film. Employing atomic modeling to study
electronic states and quantifying both electronic and phonon-assisted linkages, 
we found phonon-assisted conduction to be the major contributing factor behind
high-temperature transport in our samples. These observations reveal the presence
of interchangeable pathways for electricity and heat in nanoscale carbon-based
structures. In the context of phonon-assisted conduction, we have visually depicted 
the reciprocal space locations where energy is gained by electrons as they bridge 
gaps between near-resonant states, resulting in increased conductivity. These 
findings hold important implications for the design of future macroscopic conduction
structures that leverage room-temperature phonon-assisted conduction. These 
structures could serve as highly stable thermal energy transport conduits due to
the inherent stability of carbon materials. Furthermore, exploring the thermal
conductivity pathways of these structures may reveal novel photon-assisted conduction
mechanisms that could significantly enhance electricity transmission at lower 
temperatures. Ultimately, the development of stable, phonon-based conduits may hold
the key to achieving a unified energy transport solution for both thermal and 
electrical energy. These conduction structures could also potentially harness and 
harmoniously combine energy from both thermal and electrical conduction sources. 
In particular, the effect of combining high-temperature phonon-assisted conduction 
with low-temperature phonon-driven transport has been calculated and analyzed to 
yield substantial gains in electricity conductivity. In line with these findings, 
the structures we studied have been identified as ideal targets for phonon-assisted 
conduction experiments, while single-wall carbon nanotubes remain the only material 
suitable for direct observation of coherent electronic and phonon-assisted 
conduction mechanisms due to their inherently distinct electronic band structures. 
In our investigations, we have visually illustrated and documented the location, 
width, and temperature-dependent transitions of these phonon-assisted conduction

This study presents an efficient connectionist approach to text classification, rooted in linguistic semantics. Firstly, we introduce the concept of word sense disambiguation as a means to enhance model performance through the incorporation of semantic constraints. Secondly, we suggest the utilization of word embeddings as initial state predictions in connectionist models, thereby incorporating linguistic semantics into neural architectures. These concepts form the foundation of two novel connectionist models, namely CS-RNN and CS-LSTM, which incorporate the principles of word sense disambiguation and embeddings, and demonstrate an increase in accuracy on various datasets when compared to existing state-of-the-art sequential models. The proposed models also offer the advantage of interpretability due to their reduced number of model parameters and open-source code. Additionally, we introduce the concept of semantic regularization as a spectral regularization technique for connectionist models to enhance their performance and provide an analysis of existing text classification datasets in terms of accuracy and parameter efficiency. The experiments and analysis conducted on multiple datasets, including binary, multi-class, regression, and semantic datasets, using the proposed models confirm their efficacy. Moreover, we compare the proposed models to various existing neural architectures and demonstrate their capacity to outperform or match the performance of these models in most cases. The results validate the efficiency of the proposed connectionist models as a feature-rich classifier. in driving quantum systems is their ability to minimize any change in the system's quantum state during the driving process, effectively acting like an idle operator. However, this property holds true only as long as the driving process is not interrupted. When the driving process is disrupted, like in a binary switch scenario, the protocol's ability to maintain quantum coherence is severely compromised. This study examines the impact of the binary switch on quantum robots executing a specific quantum task and investigates strategies to recover from coherence losses caused by the switch. By applying a binary switch to a recently developed optimal CD-driven quantum robot, we demonstrate that a significant fraction of the coherence is lost and the robot's performance suffers as a result. Furthermore, we propose two potential recovery methods to mitigate the effects of the binary switch, one based on resetting the system's quantum state and the other involving the use of counterdiabatic dynamics itself. These recovery methods allow the robot to recover its optimal track, and, in our findings, we show that, in an optimal recovery scenario, the robot can successfully execute the quantum task again. Importantly, our results indicate that, even in the best case, the robot's track-following capability will always be slightly inferior to that of a CD-driven robot that executes the protocol without interruption. Our results reveal that correlations cause a significant reduction in the topological classification from $\mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ for one-dimensional systems with a single synthetic dimension, along with $\mathrm{U(1)}$ symmetry and spin-parity symmetry. Implementing virtualization using hypervisors has emerged as a suitable solution to address these demands.  Unfortunately, existing hypervisors, which were designed with general-purpose computing in mind, come with a considerable system overhead that is not suitable for mixed criticality real-time embedded systems.  Moreover, the schedulers within embedded hypervisors fail to account for the diversity of real-time scheduling needs, based largely on the principles of processor sharing.  This paper presents Tactus, a real-time hypervisor designed for mixed criticality real-time embedded systems.  Tactus offers a high level of performance by incorporating light-weight scheduling algorithms that provide flexible and customizable service rate functions.  Customizable isolation policies are implemented to meet diverse real-time scheduling needs.  This performance-focused design is supported by a small code base and is thoroughly tested for correctness and performance, backed by in-depth theoretical validation.  The practicality of Tactus is demonstrated through its successful integration with ARM Linux, which allows for the accurate measurement of hypervisor overhead.  Tactus was tested using various scenarios, which showed that the service rate function accurately reflected the demands of the scheduled processes and the overhead of the hypervisor was negligible.  Furthermore, the evaluation of Tactus revealed significant performance improvements, with up to 11 times faster processing speed in real-time hypervisors and a 68% reduction in code size compared to existing solutions.  This performance and efficiency also extend to the design of virtual CPUs, which allows for the creation of custom CPU service rate functions.  Ultimately, the design of Tactus makes it an ideal solution for real-time embedded systems of all scales and types, where meeting real-time demands is a necessity. We introduce a Zephyr Net network, which significantly surpasses the current
state-of-the-art techniques in both detection and classification capabilities for
intestinal parasite identification, while demonstrating robustness to clinical
laboratory settings and varied illumination conditions. A benchmark testing
dataset was developed with images taken from clinical settings and annotated by
medical professionals to ensure precise diagnostic accuracy. 

The Zephyr Net network boasts an advanced design that surpasses traditional
convolutional neural networks in performance. The source code for the network has
been made publicly available to facilitate future advancements in the field of
intestinal parasite detection and identification. As the area continues to grow and
develop, a testing dataset consisting of 1,800 images has been developed for
research and development purposes. 
A paper detailing the Zephyr Net network has been accepted for publication in
leading scientific journals, including the Computer Methods and Biomedical Engineering
Bulletin. A presentation detailing the network has been accepted for publication
at conferences worldwide. A patent application for the Zephyr Net network has been
submitted to the United States Patent and Tradition Office.

various types of parasites, while devising innovative and efficient methods for
parallel processing on mobile platforms, which will further contribute to the
advancement of the field. 
The comprehensive Zephyr Net network has the potential to transform clinical
diagnostic processes for intestinal parasites, ultimately saving countless lives. 
The development of an mobile application that leverages Zephyr Net's parasite
detection capabilities may aid in the identification of treatment gaps in low-income

The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.

We will instead examine a different class of timekeeping devices, based on random clicking mechanisms. A comprehensive statistical analysis framework is developed to evaluate the effectiveness of these devices, with a specific example being a single two-level atom driven coherently and monitored via photodetection, representing an extreme instance of a non-repeating clock. The statistical analysis will demonstrate that random clicking timekeeping devices can be just as precise, if not more accurate, compared to traditional devices, and their precision can even be improved by adjusting the driving strength and probability of clicking. Therefore, this article's findings offer significant insights into the realm of quantum metrology. Even more intriguingly, random clicking timekeeping devices may offer a novel approach to understanding the human perception of time. Nonetheless, the precision of channel estimation in such systems is significantly compromised by the increased risk of underutilized cyclic prefix resulting from additional cascaded RIS channels, as well as nonlinear distortions stemming from hardware imperfections. To tackle these challenges, an advanced Extreme Learning Machine (ELM)-based channel estimation method (eELM-CE) is proposed in this research to ensure accurate channel estimation. Building upon a model-driven framework, least square (LS) estimation is applied initially to highlight the linear features necessary for channel estimation. Following this step, an enhanced ELM network is created based on the identified initial features, allowing for the refinement of channel estimation. By adopting a learning-centric approach, the proposed network is empowered to better recognize nonlinear factors through activation function normalization of its data inputs. Experimental results indicate that eELM-CE outperforms existing methods by producing notably more precise estimates, as it achieves a high Symbol Error Rate (SER) of $2.58\%$ under the scenario of severely distorted signals, deep channels, long phase shifts, and undermoding conditions. Additionally, an adaptive adjustment mechanism for adjusting the network's parameters (e.g. learning rate, initial weights, and bias terms) in accordance with the changes in RIS configurations further contributes to improving the estimation accuracy. Consequently, an open-source simulation code based on this research is freely accessible on GitHub, enabling users to adjust various parameters and investigate the interactions between different system parameters in greater detail. In line with the code's utility, we also present some novel results obtained through simulations in this research. Furthermore, a set of newly created benchmark channels (e.g. Rayleigh, Rician, and Nakagami-m) were incorporated into the simulation environment to facilitate future research. These new channels are characterized by moderate levels of distortion, slower RIS phase variations, and more balanced under/over-estimation risks, as opposed to the severe underutilization of cyclic prefix resulting from deep RIS channels, highly nonlinear distortions, and undermoding conditions in the conventional Rayleigh channel. -19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 has resulted in widespread losses and socio-economic disruption, with the rapid proliferation of the virus having far-reaching effects worldwide. As part of the effort to combat this crisis, contact tracing technology, known as "Digital Contact Tracing", or "Proximity Tracing", has been hastily implemented. This technology tracks an individual's movements by monitoring their interactions with others and alerts authorities if they've been exposed to an infected person. Although a necessary measure, some versions of Digital Contact Tracing raise significant privacy concerns. This paper examines the technology, highlights its flaws, and discusses how it can be improved to avoid infringing on users' fundamental rights. The argument presented here is that Digital Contact Tracing apps should adhere to two key principles: (1) minimizing the data being collected and shared, and (2) ensuring that users are protected by robust privacy mechanisms. To validate this claim, the author reviews some of the most popular contact tracing platforms and evaluates their privacy capabilities, with a specific focus on Decentralized Privacy Preserving Proximity Tracing (DP-3T), an initiative developed by key industry figures, researchers, and healthcare experts to combat the pandemic. DP-3T's design, described here, appears to strike an optimal balance between mitigating the virus spread and safeguarding users' privacy. Furthermore, the author demonstrates how DP-3T can be adapted and applied to combat future pandemics, using the League of Necessity's proposal for measles contact tracing as a case study. The presentation of DP-3T's design is accompanied by a thorough examination of a potential key rollover attack and the secure security design review process. A new prototype, written in Swift for iOS, has also been created to illustrate an implementation of DP-3T's subeclipse protocol. A corresponding Android implementation of DP-3T is provided through the eProximityTracing project on GitHub. VACA models key aspects of a Structural Causal Model (SCM) without requiring any assumptions about its underlying parameters. VACA has several advantages over existing graph autoencoders for causal tasks: it can adapt to intricate causal graphs, train faster than existing models, generate robust predictions, and accurately computes key causal quantities. Additionally, it offers the ability to integrate new types of priors and regularization methods into its training process. Our evaluation of VACA demonstrates promising results when compared with state-of-the-art models: it matches or surpasses the performance of existing methods in predicting interventional and counterfactual scenarios, while often doing so at a significantly faster computational cost. VACA's main disadvantage lies in its limitations when dealing with causal relationships that are not inherently distinguishable from non-causal relationships in the same domain. (IoT) networks, periodic firmware updates are vital for maintaining optimal security and reliability. Given the trend towards implementing security measures via codified policy decisions and exchangeable code (security-as-a-code), these updates become increasingly analogous to push notifications for new security policies. Presently, these updates are issued uniformly to all devices, despite varying environments possessing disparate properties (e.g. different time zones, operational statuses, etc.). This uniform application may unintentionally activate undesirable effects, such as updating malicious devices before they can be removed, or applying a firmware update to a device prior to its next scheduled interval. To address these drawbacks, this research introduces a context-aware framework for targeted firmware updates, effectively acting as a firmware update tunnel, allowing specific devices to be updated based on their unique attributes and policies. Our framework is inspired by the concepts of light-weight distant fencing and secure auditing, serving as a secure proxy between manufacturers and IoT devices. When a firmware update is received, our framework assesses the device's suitability for installation by verifying its authenticity and validating its compliance with predefined policies. If the update is valid, it is processed and stored; if not, it is rejected. Our framework also incorporates a safety net to prevent devices from accepting unwanted updates and to guarantee proper rollback procedures. Our design is exemplified through the use of a Distributed Quantum Sensor Network, consisting of software-defined sensors and a firmware update proxy, used in conjunction with a Central Operating System to evaluate our approach. An in-depth analysis of our framework is conducted through simulations, exploring the intersection of device authentication and policy decision mechanisms, as well as reverse engineering and potential exploitation of manufacturing code. These simulations highlight the efficacy and practicality of our design framework. Our code is openly source and may be accessed at https://github.com/mascolo-andrea/firmware_tunnel.git. Given the inherent complexity of this problem, we address it by decomposing the system into two subspaces based on the occupation numbers of the sub-energetic states, enabling us to develop computationally efficient methods. We calculate the propagator and self-energy for non-occupied states in the upper energy level, then use these results to derive effective expressions for the lower occupied states. Our results utilize a decomposition of the time-evolution operator into its non-occupied and charged components, allowing us to formulate the problem as a set of coupled equations for the non-occupied sector. Additionally, we establish a constraint by the total magnetic field flux through the spatial infinity, effectively preventing time-evolution from leading to occupation of the non-occupied energy level. With these results, we are able to compute the dynamics of spin-$1/2$ fermions in the presence of time-varying magnetic fields, applicable to both atomic and quark systems, and could significantly impact our understanding of quantum systems with oscillating magnetic properties. Moreover, we outline the necessary conditions for applying our solution, given the periodicity of the time-evolution. It suffices to monitor the cumulative flux of the instantaneous magnetic field over one period. If the total flux is minimal, the system will experience a non-adiabatic, highly chaotic dynamics, whereas a moderate to high total flux will result in occupation of the non-occupied energy level and return to its ground state via a quantum transition. However, if the total flux is low, the system will experience an adiabatic, non-chaotic dynamics, and will not reach the non-occupied energy level. Detailed analytical expressions are calculated for the dynamics of spin-$1/2$ fermions in the absence of external magnetic fields, applicable to atomic systems with oscillating magnetic properties, and are consistent with existing results in the literature. Additionally, we have developed an open-source (golang) generator of, and solver for, the time-evolution of spin-$1/2$ fermions in the presence of time-varying magnetic fields, which can address a broad range of general cases. This code is available at the address https://example.com/solve. Here, we present the necessary and sufficient conditions for the dynamics of spin-$1/2$ fermions in the presence of time-varying magnetic fields, and have formulated an algorithm to determine these conditions.

As turbulence intensity diminishes, a critical transition occurs where Reynolds and molecular thermal fluctuations swap prominence in momentum transport. Utilizing the theoretical framework of Edwards and Landau, we calculate the variance of velocity components for both fully developed turbulence and temporally decaying flows. Our calculations reveal that temperature correlations retain a non-zero limit even in the absence of Reynolds fluctuations, thereby providing an additional contribution to momentum transport. Essentially, this indicates that temperature correlations serve as a significant factor in momentum transport throughout the entire turbulent regime, consistent with prior observations. Prior many-body turbulence theories have substantiated the role of temperature correlations in momentum transport; in this revised work, we determine a practical, numerically computable expression for temperature's contribution to momentum transport. To validate our theoretical predictions, we analyze data from direct numerical simulations of isotropic turbulence and decaying homogeneous turbulence, revealing substantial agreement between our predictions and experimental data. Furthermore, to pinpoint the optimal simulation settings for accurate predictions, we evaluate various turbulent configurations. This study presents an in-depth numerical analysis that accurately simulates the thermal behavior of the fluid and its impact on laser interactions. Though past research mainly focused on the resonant production mode of these hypothetical particles, new findings have uncovered a diverse and complex phenomenology associated with the non-resonant diagrams at narrow widths. In this study, we thoroughly examine the influence of the non-resonant diagrams on the single production topologies of Top and Bottom companions and their impact on estimating total production rates. We also introduce a novel method for determining the non-resonant amplitude from data fitting and establish a relationship between the non-resonant and resonant amplitudes. Additionally, we investigate how the non-resonant diagrams affect the detection strategies of Top and Bottom companions. We discover that, when the non-resonant diagrams are considered, the single production topologies become even more significant than initially thought, while the single Bottom production topology becomes more prominent than previously estimated, requiring specialized algorithms to separate its contributions. We also demonstrate that the non-resonant diagrams enable the measurement of Bottom companions using single muons and Bottom tagging when considering the various Bottom masses and lifetimes. Furthermore, we show that the single production topology's significance is slightly reduced when the non-resonant diagrams are involved, while the single Bottom production topology remains a potential powerful indicator of additional Bottom companions. Lastly, we outline the prospects of identifying a hypothetical Top companion through single production topologies at the HL-LHC and a future hadronic collider. The study provides a comprehensive understanding of the single production topologies at the HL-LHC and a future hadronic collider when the non-resonant diagrams are taken into account. It suggests that the single production topology at the HL-LHC remains a valuable tool for estimating the combined rate of Top companions. However, at a future hadronic collider with enhanced particle identification capabilities, the combined rate can be determined with greater precision, accompanied by a greater sensitivity to suppress the overwhelming background of QCD multijet events. Specifically, the study determines that at the HL-LHC, a Top companion with a 50 GeV mass and 1 fb$^{-1}$ of data can be detected with a 95% confidence level when considering the single production topologies, while at a future hadronic collider with 100 fb$^{-1}$ of data and enhanced particle identification capabilities, such a Top companion can be identified with a 95% confidence level when the combined rate of Top companions is as low as 0.2 fb. When encountering questions about new knowledge resources, classes, or properties, these models fall short, making them ineffective beyond their training scope. Leveraging the success achieved in other areas of natural language processing, we developed an innovative approach that involves introducing a mechanism to copy elements directly from questions. "Chinese Whispers" game, where agents communicate through noisy messages to infer each other's labels. Building on the deterministic Chinese Whispers algorithm by Funk, Demaine, and Shah, our probabilistic models provide a more accurate statistical framework for understanding label inference in complex networks, even with incorrect connections. Initially, we examined two separate models for agent communication: a simple model that uses a uniform noise distribution, and a complex model with noise based on agent characteristics. Both models were tested with real-world data from three distinct networks, and our results show how incorporating probability can improve the accuracy of label guesses compared to the deterministic approach. Next, we presented a probabilistic model that accounts for agent interactions and noise by applying a Bayesian inference formula to infer labels from network activity patterns, agent properties, and communication data. By applying this model to a Facebook social network, our analysis reveals the most likely agent labels and their corresponding probability distribution. Additionally, our work involves computing the Whispers correlation distance - a measure of similarity between agent pairs based on their inferred labels - for various networks, including Facebook, Twitter, and three Facebook networks specific to distinct geographical regions, providing a novel insight into their structure. Lastly, our investigation into the properties of Whispers correlation distance across different networks suggests that this metric can effectively distinguish between network types, making it a valuable tool for analyzing social networks, particularly those with hidden patterns or classified data sets. All mathematical and computational aspects of our work are detailed in order to facilitate reproduction of the results. Our findings highlight the significance of leveraging probabilistic models for understanding complex social networks, a approach that we anticipate will be crucial for both current and future data sets. Further, our model with multi-agent interactions can be generalized to incorporate additional factors such as variable noise, agent context, and network topology by applying the Bayesian inference principle, providing a valuable framework for analyzing hidden patterns or classified data sets. The derived Whispers correlation distance can be utilized to distinguish between different network types including social networks, network combinations, community structures, and network correlations. We specifically address the problem of estimating a matrix of rank one from observations with differing Gaussian noise levels across various matrix components. We derive exact formulas for the mean squared error in matrix and factor estimation in an infinite-dimensional setting where a fixed number of matrix components is considered. These findings are based on an innovative model transformation from the homogeneous to a heterogeneous low-rank matrix model in conjunction with a newly proposed information-theoretic approach to analyzing matrix estimation problems. We demonstrate that this approach allows us to pinpoint the information-theoretic limit of matrix estimation, and we believe that its value extends beyond this specific context. We also show that this limit can be achieved in a technically challenging scenario of matrix observation under quadratic loss. Furthermore, we apply this approach to a broader class of matrix estimation problems, including supersymmetric, Gaussian, and Erdos-Renyi matrices, and to the problem of covariate shift adaptation, showing that our approach can yield precise, previously unknown analysis results for these scenarios. Finally, we propose a set of sensing matrices, referred to as twisted Gaussian matrices, which offer improved performance in comparison to standard Gaussian matrices in matrix estimation problems. These sensing matrices address a particular matrix estimation problem but may also have applications in multiple other contexts of matrix estimation with a low-rank structure where Gaussian sensing matrices are commonly used. We further investigate the applicability of this set of sensing matrices in matrix multiplication, rank estimation, and related problems and analyze their potential limitations, ultimately concluding that a subset of this set lies within the information-theoretic limit of these tasks. We propose a set of methods, named robust zeroth-order optimization (RZO), which is capable of efficiently solving a broad class of real-valued non-convex optimization problems, including well-known issues like non-convex optimization, which is a hot topic in machine learning, and optimization in complex architectures like neural networks with gate functions that are highly non-smooth and non-convex. We further show that our method is compatible with various types of optimization algorithms in both non-convex and convex settings, which we demonstrate by providing, as an example, a RZO version of the gradient descent algorithm for non-convex optimization, which is a widely used method in this domain. We have found that this method is directly related to a well-known optimization technique called as quasisecant algorithm, which we show to be a subset of RZO,

By incorporating inverse gate implementations, noise levels are diminished and the robustness of the quantum circuit improves. This strategy proves particularly efficacious in scenarios where a quantum subroutine can be inverted, such as when compiling gates from two-qubit interactions that require robustness. A crucial advantage arises from the fact that the inverse gate is implemented using the very same gates used to compute its original counterpart, thus ensuring optimal performance. As a concrete demonstration, our approach significantly enhances the performance of a mixed-phase quantum simulation algorithm, leading to substantial reductions in qubit counts for simulations of quantum systems, either when considering NISQ noise models or noiseless implementations. Furthermore, our method renders the quantum circuit fully classical-sampling, enabling the implementation of classical shadows, a technique that has been hindered by the need for positive-semidefinite matrices in its original formulation. The concepts underlying our method also facilitate a novel method for estimating the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, which could be the basis for developing future quantum algorithms. Lastly, our technique proves effective in counteracting both closed-system and open-system coherent errors, demonstrating its versatility in addressing a wide range of error types. Despite its versatility, the primary value of our method lies in its ability to accelerate VQA by incorporating the inverse method. This insight is particularly relevant because inverse gates are inherently noise-reducing and can be implemented with minimal additional overhead. When applied to a specific scenario, our method not only boosts the robustness of the circuit but also achieves this with fewer qubits, essentially providing a tradeoff between circuit robustness and qubit count. The potential applications of our research extend to accelerating any VQA that can benefit from the hidden inverse method, with future investigations to be conducted on more advanced quantum algorithms. One such potential extension involves the application of our method to accelerate a recent recombination-based approach to quantum simulation. To implement this idea, our method would necessitate inverting the evolution between basis states, a scenario that poses a significant challenge to current quantum computing capabilities. Notably, our method also facilitates a novel method, which estimates the BCH expansion by representing the Hamiltonian as a matrix whose powers are bounded by a basis of maximally coupled terms. This technique could, in turn, be used to develop an efficient classical algorithm for determining the quantum state after a long, time-varying evolution. A template-based approach is used to compare and combine wind and wave data from satellites and historical forecasts. Analysis involves standardizing wind and wave measurements and applying an extreme value model to estimate the probability of severe storms in specific locations. Results from this investigation reveal a significant decline in extreme weather correlations among Metop satellite wind speeds, wave forecasts, and wave measurements over a range of 600 to 800 kilometers. To compare the effectiveness of satellite and forecast wave height predictions, an alternative approach involving wave interpolation and error analysis is employed. By integrating spatial analysis and extreme value methods, this study provides a deeper understanding of satellite and forecast wave observations and their differences. Furthermore, this research shows that combining information from satellites and models can improve the comprehension of wave behavior and provide valuable insights into the properties of ocean waves. Finally, by quantifying the advantages and disadvantages of using satellites and models together, this study offers a framework for integrating data from various sources to enhance our knowledge of ocean wave dynamics. In particular, it highlights the potential in using satellites as a bridge between model outputs and direct wave measurements to infer accurate wave behavior. It is also demonstrated that combining spatial data and temporal data significantly improves the effectiveness of extreme weather pattern analysis at different scales. By modeling the relationship between satellite and forecast data at separate locations using spatial methods, this study shows that accounting for these relationships significantly improves the ability to forecast extreme weather patterns and eliminates spatial irregularities in the data. Finally, it was found that eliminating the correlations between satellite and forecast data actually improves the effectiveness of extreme weather forecasts and reduces biases in the predictions. In contrast, in the case of wave height observations, it was discovered that eliminating the correlations between satellites and forecasts slightly decreases the effectiveness of wave height forecasts and introduces biases in the predictions. These results highlight the significance of considering spatial relationships in data integration and prediction, especially when extreme events are involved. They also confirm the potential of using satellites as a bridge between model outputs and direct observations to improve our understanding of ocean wave dynamics when considering data from various sources together. In particular, in the case of wave height analysis, it was found that combining data from satellites and models significantly improves the ability to infer wave behavior and reduce biases in the predictions. Despite this, developing a full-fledged model for each specific disease is impractical, thus class-based transfer learning becomes a feasible option. However, both methods have their own limitations when dealing with unsupervised semantic segmentation tasks.

This study examines the effectiveness of both full-model and transfer learning-based approaches for unsupervised semantic segmentation in multi-label medical images. The authors conduct an extensive meta-analysis of 122 datasets from various fields to identify patterns and trends among different classification and segmentation methods, augmentation techniques, loss functions, and regularization strategies. A statistical model analyzing the relationship between training resources and test performance is also presented.

Key findings from this study include:

1. For each dataset, comparing full-model and transfer learning-based approaches shows transfer learning generally achieves higher mIoU test scores, suggesting transfer learning is a more efficient starting point for unsupervised learning in medical image image segmentation tasks.
2. Both methods demonstrate significant room for improvement, with many datasets achieving above 80% mIoU test scores only after rigorous training and advanced architecture implementations.
3. A linear relationship between training data and test performance is observed, indicating better resource utilization can notably boost performance.
4. Insights from this study can inform future unsupervised learning designs to improve the efficiency and quality of medical image segmentation tasks.

This study provides comprehensive insights into unsupervised learning in medical image segmentation, offering valuable guidance for developers of fully automatic image classification systems to improve their designs and performance. Due to its extensive meta-analysis and participatory structure, this study offers far more comprehensive insights than typical surveys in the field. Notably, given the open-access nature of the study, more data can be added to further enhance its utility, making it a dynamic resource for continued research in the field. A web-based database of the analysis results can be accessed at https://lnls.github.io/unsup-miigs-ma/, with the underlying code available at https://github.com/lnls/unsup-miigs-ma. 

It's worth noting that an updated version of the study has been submitted as a journal publication at the time of writing.

While commonly regarded as cumbersome, we argue that alternative methods of adding a clock exist, with varying levels of intrusion. We present a new approach that simplifies termination proofs without overly utilizing the clock mechanism, particularly illustrated through the context of functional big-step semantics for programming language interpretations.  To enforce termination, a clock is added as an auxiliary function that decreases for each function call, generally with the exception of fundamental data types and function application. Furthermore, our findings suggest that local news COVID coverage varied based on the political affiliation of their audiences, with Republican-leaning audiences having seen more COVID coverage in the initial stages. A parallel was observed between North Carolina's presidential primary and a significant spike in COVID coverage, followed by a sustained high rate of coverage in the state throughout the data collection period. These findings underscore the complex interplay of local, political, and non-local factors that influenced COVID news coverage, highlighting the importance of tailored public health approaches and potential implications for vaccine hesitancy and the emerging omicron variant. The emerging pandemic waves have once again underscored the pivotal role local media play in disseminating public health information, making our research highly relevant for future public health communications approaches. The data and code used for this study are publicly available for replication and exploration. Through close monitoring of local news, our study can be easily updated to provide timely and precise insights on the residual COVID-related skepticism and the evolving pandemic landscape. Moreover, the analysis of news coverage on other public health and science issues offers a wealth of knowledge for developing effective health communication strategies to combat misinformation and promote targeted interventions among various demographics. The approach in this study can be applied to various topics such as vaccination, climate change, and genetics to understand and analyze contemporary science controversies. The analysis provides structured evidence on the perceived credibility of science and technologies that can be measured across different contexts to assess their reputation and the dynamics of public perception over time. The study explores the correlations between U.S. state death rates and news coverage of COVID in the latter half of 2020, with results showing that local news coverage was initially driven by national death rates, exhibiting a positive correlation at 0.22 (p < 0.01). Moreover, our analysis found that state-level variations in COVID coverage and death rates were independent of population size, implying that smaller local news outlets played a critical role in the transmission of public health information

To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Consequently, this research implies that, unless attitudes towards novelty resume their pre-pandemic patterns, the pandemic may have a lasting, negative impact on urban diversity. It also highlights the significance of leveraging data-driven research to inform policies promoting diversity and vitality in urban environments. Such studies can guide policy decisions in two main ways: 1) recommendations that directly address individuals or organisations to promote diversity and vitality, and 2) advisory roles in designing recovery strategies from crises similar to the one caused by the pandemic.
